report:
**Conclusion: no—the evidence does not support that answer.** Offering HIV self-testing *in addition to* usual testing options generally causes more people to test for HIV, at least in the settings studied.

The strongest evidence is a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials (13 in sub-Saharan Africa). Compared with standard HIV-testing services alone, adding/offering self-testing **doubled HIV-test uptake** in the general population. Effects appeared across several delivery approaches and levels of user support.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589537021002716

A separate systematic review/meta-analysis focused on African adults likewise concluded that HIV self-testing has potential to increase testing uptake versus standard services. However, it found lower linkage to care/antiretroviral treatment after a reactive self-test in the available studies—an important qualification: more testing is beneficial only if confirmatory testing and care are made easy.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33503050/

WHO’s evidence update describes HIV self-testing as a safe, accurate, effective option to reach people who might otherwise not test, including key populations, men, and young people.  
https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36

So the defensible interpretation is: **yes, an additional offer of HIV self-testing increases uptake overall**, rather than simply substituting for facility testing. But results are context-dependent (most randomized evidence was from sub-Saharan Africa), self-reported testing can affect measurement, and implementation must include clear routes to confirmatory testing, prevention, and treatment.
